exercise.name: Dumbbell Pendlay Row

reference.title: Dumbbell Pendlay Row
reference.listing: Video; data sheet: body part Back, equipment Dumbbell, exercise type Strength

exercise.mechanics: Compound (shoulder extension, scapular retraction, elbow flexion)

breathing.pattern: Brace at the dead stop, exhale through the fast pull, inhale as you lower to the floor.
breathing.cadence: About 0.6 s up, short squeeze, 1.2 s down, 1.2 s dead stop

prescription.tempo: Explosive up, 1 s down, dead stop on the floor
prescription.load: User-chosen dumbbells; stop about 2 reps short of failure (RIR 2) or when the trunk starts to rise
prescription.progression: Add load, keeping the trunk still

cues.text: Hinge until the back is nearly level, knees bent, dumbbells resting on the floor under the shoulders; brace.
Row both dumbbells fast to the lower ribs, elbows driving back; the trunk does not move.
Squeeze the shoulder blades together for a moment.
Lower under control until the dumbbells touch the floor.
Dead stop: let the dumbbells rest on the floor, re-brace, then pull again.

mistakes.mistake: Lifting the chest to swing the weight up
mistakes.fix: The back stays level; only the arms and shoulder blades move.

mistakes.mistake: Bouncing the dumbbells off the floor
mistakes.fix: Come to a full stop on every rep.

mistakes.mistake: Rounding the back to reach the floor
mistakes.fix: Bend the knees more so the dumbbells reach the floor with a flat back.

kinematics.norm: Back nearly level, held still (clinical opinion)
Knees bent enough for the dumbbells to reach the floor with a flat back (clinical opinion)
From straight to about 90 degrees at the top (clinical opinion)
Fast pull, controlled lowering, full stop on the floor (clinical opinion)

sources.title: GymVisual #1188712, Dumbbell Pendlay Row, video (movement reference)
Fenwick, Brown & McGill 2009, comparison of different rowing exercises: trunk muscle activation and lumbar spine motion, load and stiffness (J Strength Cond Res 23(2):350-358)
Lehman et al. 2004, variations in muscle activation levels during traditional latissimus dorsi weight training exercises (Dynamic Medicine 3:4)

cautions: Stop if sharp pain, numbness, tingling or giving-way occurs.
The dumbbell load is your choice: pick a weight you can move with the form shown for every rep.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
Low-back pain: the level trunk loads the back heavily; a bench-supported row is gentler (Fenwick 2009).
modify: Tight hamstrings: bend the knees more or set the dumbbells on low blocks.
regressions: Dumbbell bent-over row with a more upright trunk.

muscleNotes.lats_r: Main shoulder extensor: pulls the elbow from below the shoulder back beside the trunk.
muscleNotes.lats_l: Main shoulder extensor: pulls the elbow from below the shoulder back beside the trunk.
muscleNotes.rhomboids_midtrap_r: Squeeze the shoulder blade back at the top; rows gave the highest middle trapezius/rhomboid activity of the pulls tested by Lehman 2004.
muscleNotes.rhomboids_midtrap_l: Squeeze the shoulder blade back at the top; rows gave the highest middle trapezius/rhomboid activity of the pulls tested by Lehman 2004.
muscleNotes.post_deltoid_r: Helps extend the shoulder as the elbow passes the trunk.
muscleNotes.post_deltoid_l: Helps extend the shoulder as the elbow passes the trunk.
muscleNotes.biceps_r: Flexes the elbow; the neutral grip shares the work with brachialis and brachioradialis.
muscleNotes.biceps_l: Flexes the elbow; the neutral grip shares the work with brachialis and brachioradialis.
muscleNotes.spinal_extensors_r: Hold the trunk near level with a flat back for every rep; the standing bent-over row placed the highest lumbar load of the rows in Fenwick 2009.
muscleNotes.spinal_extensors_l: Hold the trunk near level with a flat back for every rep; the standing bent-over row placed the highest lumbar load of the rows in Fenwick 2009.
